American consumers are becoming increasingly bullish on equities:

The perceived probability among US consumers that US stock prices will be higher 1-year from now increased +2.9 percentage points in June, to 40.9%, the highest since April 2021.

This is also the 3rd-highest reading since the 2020 pandemic recovery.

By age, consumers under 40 are the most optimistic, at 43.1%, the highest since May 2021.

This is followed by the 40-59 and over 59 age groups, both at 40.2%, the highest readings this year.

By income, the perceived probability of higher stock prices rose to 48.3% among those earning over $100,000, the highest since January 2025.

This compares with 38.6% among those earning $50,000-$100,000 and 33.6% among those earning under $50,000, both in-line with the average over the last 2 years.

High-income American consumers are historically bullish.

The BIP-110 sentiment data clearly touched a nerve.

That's ok.

Novel datasets have a way of doing that. The point of the post was not to settle the debate. It was to show a measurable divergence in how each side has been speaking over time.

Mixed in with the heat, I did get a couple good questions:

1) "Dude, have you run the same analysis on those opposing bip110? If not, that's one of many reasons that this is useless."

This is a really good question as it's the contrast between these two groups that's most interesting.

The results (shown below) indicate that the Anti-BIP-110 cohort has had much higher levels of conviction over the exact same duration of time that the Pro-BIP-110 cohort has had lower levels of conviction.

2) "Bro makes up 4-year conviction metric on a BIP that was proposed 9 months ago?"

This tracks conviction language across the posting history of accounts now associated with each side of the debate.

Gold = Above Baseline.

Blue = Below Baseline.

So yes, there is four years of sentiment data. 

I show that wide of a range so you can visualize just how dramatically these groups have shifted since BIP-110 was proposed in October 2025. 

Since then, individuals in the Pro-BIP-110 cohort have shown much lower than average conviction, while individuals in the Anti-BIP-110 cohort have shown much higher than average conviction.

This doesn't fundamentally tell us how things will play out, but it does give some clues to the underlying moods of each individual group.

3) "Guy doesn’t disclose who it tracks and what conviction actually measures?"

I’ve discussed the methodology publicly for a while now and explained in writing/podcasts how I collect and categorize this data. I have links to my archive in my bio for anyone who wants to understand the framework more deeply.

Gold is entering a historically favorable period of the year:

Gold prices have gained +1.5% in July on average over the last 20 years, making it the 2nd-strongest month of the year.

Gold prices have also recorded positive returns in 65% of July months, the 2nd-best win rate of any month.

The strongest July over this period was in 2020, when gold returned +10.7%.

The only better month historically has been August, with an average gain of +1.6% since 2005.

August also posted a 55% win rate, with its strongest year coming in 2011, when gold returned +12.1%.

By comparison, June has historically been the weakest month, with an average decline of -0.4% and just 40% positive readings since 2005.

Seasonality is turning in favor of gold bulls.

I've mostly avoided any involvement in the BIP-110 debate, but the language/sentiment data I've explored is too interesting not to share.

One of the sentiment metrics I watch closely is "conviction".

This is basically measuring the amount of confidence in someone's language over time (gold line).

The inverse of this is hedging (blue line), which shows up when people are less confident or put more qualifiers around how they speak.

In the chart below, you can visualize the language data for these most active BIP-110 supporters I've tracked over the last four years. 

Their confidence has fallen sharply.

This is in direct contrast to other cohorts I track, like MSTR investors, who (despite the negative price action) have actually been growing more convicted recently.

Interestingly, the lowest levels of conviction for this group happen precisely around the time that BIP-110 was officially proposed in October 2025.

So the takeaway IMO is not simply "BIP-110 folks are not confident they will succeed".

Conviction is related to the stories we tell ourselves.

We use stories as a way to make sense of the world, when stories crumble, so too does our conviction.

With that idea in mind, I believe the story driving this group came under pressure. This is evident in that rapid downturn in the amount of conviction they expressed throughout 2025.

Although their net conviction is slowly climbing back up from the lows, this group still remains much less confident than the broader Bitcoin ecosystem during a time where tensions and arguments are heating up.

I'm going to keep watching this closely. But regardless of what happens over the coming weeks, this data shows that Bitcoin debates are never purely technical. 

Even when the conversation focuses on code, policy, or protocol details, there are emotional and human dynamics lurking beneath the surface that are impossible to escape from.
